word_order: SVO | Subject-Verb-Object order seen throughout (e.g. "The game is based ...", "Blood goes away from the heart ...", "Arthur Guinness signed ...").
register: Mostly written, formal expository (encyclopedic/news style) with occasional instructions (safety/advice); not spontaneous conversational speech.
non_boundary_traps: commas inside appositives or enumerations (e.g. "Korean, Thai, Indian, and Japanese" or "The comments, live on television, ...")
parenthetical abbreviations and alternate names in parentheses (e.g. "Daesh (ISIL)")
commas after introductory adverbials (e.g. "Although in the end,")
commas between adjectives or prepositional modifiers (e.g. "shorter than the foot, with straighter phalanges")
unstable_prefix_signals: which — marks a relative clause or non-restrictive comment that attaches to the preceding noun phrase; translating before seeing the clause risks wrong structure/attachment in Chinese
that — introduces a clausal complement or restrictive clause; early split often prevents proper Chinese clause restructuring
called — often begins a postnominal naming/appositive phrase ("...towers, called ziggurats,") which should usually stay with the noun
such as / especially / including — introduce examples or sublists; the scope of the examples (and whether to render as examples or as part of the head noun) is unresolved until the list completes
left parenthesis '(' — signals an immediate appositive/alternate name or abbreviation that affects how the preceding token should be rendered
comma immediately followed by a noun phrase and another comma (apposition pattern ", NP, ") — indicates the preceding NP has an appositive that must be attached
semicolon ';' used to separate complex list items — indicates a continued coordinated structure whose full translation depends on later items
dash/em dash '—' or hyphen used to introduce an imperative or sudden clause — the relation to the preceding fragment is often revision-prone
target_transfer_hazards: parenthetical aliases/abbreviations like "(ISIL)" or any '(' opening — the Chinese rendering (use both names, one name, or a parenthetical translation) cannot be decided until the parenthesis content is seen
relative pronouns 'which' / 'that' — Chinese relative clause placement/marker choice depends on the full relative clause that follows
postnominal 'called' phrases — whether to render as apposition or integrated name depends on the following token(s)

comma-separated enumerations (list items separated by commas) and semicolon-separated lists — you cannot finalize punctuation/connector choices in Chinese until you know whether the list continues or ends
appositive pattern ", NP," — whether to translate as an aside/apposition or as part of the main NP is unresolved until the closing comma/phrase appears
dashes introducing new clauses or imperatives — the role (explanation, emphasis, instruction) is only clear once the dash-bound material is seen
notes_for_prompt_writer: Keep default segmentation after simple finite clauses (SVO main clauses) but avoid splitting immediately after nouns or verbs when any of the unstable_prefix_signals appear. Treat parentheses, 'called', 'which/that' relative markers, 'such as' and comma/semicolon-separated lists as signals to delay emitting a segment until the whole apposition/relative/listing material is available. For Chinese output, prefer to keep a head noun together with its postnominal modifiers (appositives, relative clauses, 'called' phrases) in the same translation unit.

target_language_profile.word_order: Basic SVO. Modifiers (adjectives, quantifiers, relative clauses) generally precede nouns. Topic-comment structures common; some fronting permitted but core constituent order relatively rigid.
target_language_profile.verb_placement: Verb follows subject, precedes object. Aspect/resultative complements and particles are post-verbal, so aspect, resultatives, serial verbs and object/topic choice must often be deferred.
late_commitment_forced_by: postnominal relative clauses in source (Chinese places relative clause before the noun)
aspectual information and resultative complements that appear after main verb or later clauses
serial or multi-verb predicates whose internal structure appears later
numeral + noun when classifier choice depends on the specific noun
attachment ambiguities (which clause/adverbial attaches to which verb) changing topicalization or word order
scope of negation, modals, or tense auxiliaries revealed later in sentence
target_language_profile.reordering_vs_source: Frequent reordering: source postnominal relatives → pre-nominal, modifiers move before noun, adverbials often earlier, objects may topicalize to sentence-initial position, prepositional semantics often become pre-verbal coverb phrases.
safe_boundary_signals: source provides main verb plus all auxiliaries/complements and clause termination
head noun plus any following relative clause or modifiers already completed
explicit numeral followed immediately by the noun (classifier choice known)
unsafe_boundary_signals: after hearing only the subject but no verb or auxiliaries
after a noun that may be followed by a relative pronoun/clause (e.g., 'the book' before 'that/which/who')
after a numeral without the following noun (classifier choice unknown)
after prepositional/subordinating conjunctions when attachment target unclear
after main verb but before clause-final particles or resultatives that alter aspect
